dailyBrief.text: Big night ahead, Cleveland: the Guardians face elimination in ALCS Game 6 at Tampa Bay at 8 PM, after Tampa Bay took Sunday's Game 5, 3–1, for a 3–2 series lead. The Browns gave you a walk-off win yesterday — 13–10 over Baltimore and a share of first place — so the city starts the week in a fighting mood. Overnight, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting St. Petersburg oil sites ablaze, while Washington argued over intelligence sharing and the Russia sanctions waiver. Solon woke up clear and frosty at 34°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 67°. Tonight in town: Solon Council votes on the park and trail notes, the Jonas Brothers play Rocket Arena, and the Cleveland Orchestra trio performs at Severance — both shows at 7:30.

weekBrief.text: It's a classic crisp fall week in Solon: dry and sunny almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s — good weather for getting outside and for playoff baseball. The Guardians need two wins in Florida to reach the World Series, with a possible Game 7 Tuesday and the Series itself starting Friday. The Browns take their share of first place to Tennessee on Sunday, the Cavs open at Philadelphia on Thursday and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and Ohio State gets a bye to heal up at quarterback after Saturday's win at Indiana. Around town: trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama campaigns in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and the baby countdown is very much on, so it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

Kremlin hawks enjoy the Trump-Zelenskiy rift — but Moscow is not celebrating yet
items.summary:
Hard-liners in Moscow are publicly enjoying a rough week for Ukraine's president, after President Trump repeatedly criticized Volodymyr Zelenskiy and at one point said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev mocked Zelenskiy on Telegram, and a Kremlin economic envoy reposted an image suggesting Russia and the United States now stand together against Britain and Europe.

Reuters reports the satisfaction in Moscow is cautious rather than triumphant. Russian officials still see Trump as unpredictable, European leaders rallied behind Zelenskiy at a summit last week, most American sanctions on Russia remain in place, and Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian targets have not stopped.

That caution matters because it cuts against the idea that the public split automatically hands Moscow a win. If Washington's position shifts again, or Europe fills more of the gap, the advantage Russia appears to have gained this week could shrink quickly.

Analysts quoted in the reporting also see Trump's moves partly through the lens of the November midterms at home — one more reason Moscow is keeping the champagne, as Reuters put it, on ice.

items.title: France moves to help riot-hit shops and add police, as arrests reach about 2,400
items.summary:
France spent Monday counting the cost of its worst weekend of unrest in years and trying to prevent a repeat. The government says more than 3,000 shops were pillaged or damaged, the historic town hall in Limoges was torched, and roughly 2,400 people were arrested as protests over living costs and underfunded public services turned violent in cities across the country.

Mayors of the biggest cities demanded answers from the government on Monday, saying preparations were inadequate. In response, officials are arranging partial curfews in some places, promising more police on the ground if protests return next weekend, and setting up state-backed furlough help so damaged businesses can avoid layoffs while they recover. Insurers are expected to cover part of the losses, though the funding details are not yet complete.

Investigators are reviewing online video to identify looters, and prosecutors have also opened inquiries into serious injuries to protesters, including teenagers hurt in Saint-Etienne and Mulhouse. That second track means policing tactics, not just rioter violence, will be under scrutiny.

Calm had largely returned to the streets by Monday. Whether it holds depends on whether the government's support package and a promised roundtable with students, teachers and unions land before the next weekend of planned action.

items.title: Rubio in Central Asia: Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending the war
items.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, traveling in Uzbekistan, said Monday that Ukraine and Russia should be focused on ending their war, and he downplayed talk of a possible three-way meeting involving Presidents Trump, Putin and Xi. Rubio said there had been talk of a meeting but he did not know whether it had been finalized, adding that Trump has been clear he wants the war to end.

Rubio landed in Samarkand on Sunday night for meetings with the C5+1 group — the United States plus Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. Trump hosted those leaders at the White House last November, and the trip keeps Central Asia, a region where Russia and China both compete for influence, on Washington's agenda.

Rubio warned that the war carries a real risk of spreading if a sabotage attempt fails or drones knocked off course wander into a neighboring country. That warning came as a fresh Russian air strike killed a woman in Kyiv overnight and damaged a subway station and a 25-story residential building, according to the reporting.

The United States has been trying to mediate an end to the war, and Trump has paired that effort with a diesel import deal with Russia and a waiver of some sanctions — moves Zelenskiy has criticized, and which now sit at the center of the Washington-Kyiv dispute.

items.title: Ukraine's huge drone barrage still reverberates, a day after St. Petersburg oil fires
items.summary:
Ukraine's weekend attack — more than 1,000 drones sent at targets across Russia — remains the military backdrop to Monday's diplomacy. Fires broke out at an oil export terminal and an oil depot in St. Petersburg, and Russian officials said one person was killed and several others were wounded.

Russia's defense ministry said it destroyed 1,015 drones across 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea. The strikes were not limited to military sites: a large retail logistics center and a technology company's data center were also confirmed hit or burning, which is part of why the attack drew so much attention inside Russia.

Kyiv's case is that Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian energy sites — Zelenskiy says dozens of times in the past week alone — despite talk of an energy ceasefire. Washington, meanwhile, has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure even as it tries to broker talks.

Watch how the scale of this strike is used by each side this week: Kyiv as leverage, Moscow as justification, and Washington as an argument in the sanctions debate.

items.title: China grows 4.5% in the third quarter — strong factories, weak property, and Asia markets steadied
items.summary:
China reported Monday that its economy expanded 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, a touch ahead of forecasts and up from 4.3% in the spring. Growth for the first nine months is 4.6%, inside Beijing's full-year target range, helped by stronger factory output and retail sales in September.

The weak spots are unchanged: investment fell sharply over the first nine months and property spending dropped by about a fifth. Exports, by contrast, have stayed strong enough to push the trade surplus toward record territory — the classic two-speed picture of an economy leaning on foreign buyers while households stay cautious.

Asia markets took the number as an anchor on a nervous day. South Korea's KOSPI erased an early 3% rout to close higher, and Tokyo and Taipei pared steep opening losses after Wall Street's tech slide, with chipmaker TSMC finishing flat after being down sharply at the open.

With the annual target still in reach, the data reduce pressure for a big new stimulus package, though targeted help for home buyers and local governments is expected to continue.

items.title: Super Typhoon Champi strengthens back toward Category 5 as Guam restores most power lines
items.summary:
The storm that brushed Guam over the weekend is getting stronger again over open water. After passing about ten miles south of the island at Category 4 strength, Champi re-intensified in the Philippine Sea, and forecasters placed it roughly 470 miles west of Guam on Monday with sustained winds around 160 mph.

On Guam itself, the recovery bulletin was comparatively good news: about 90% of transmission lines restored, all substations energized and roughly 70% of feeder circuits back, though schools closed Monday for damage inspections and some electricity, water and health services remained disrupted. The island lost about half its power at the storm's peak, and no deaths were reported.

Champi is forecast to keep strengthening through Tuesday before gradually weakening, on a track toward waters south of Okinawa and near Taiwan around October 22 to 24. It is expected to enter the Philippine area of responsibility on Tuesday, where it will be named Rosal.

For Guam, the next phase is cleanup and full restoration. For Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands, the watch now is the exact track — models still diverge after midweek.

items.title: Three new polls put Trump's approval at new lows, with the economy as his main vulnerability
items.summary:
A trio of national surveys released over the weekend — from Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos, NBC News and Fox News — point the same direction: President Trump's approval has hit new lows, and Democrats lead Republicans by roughly 8 to 10 points ahead of the midterms, according to Axios reporting summarized Monday morning.

The striking shift is on the economy. Axios described it as the president's main vulnerability — an issue that helped him win in 2024 and now ranks among his biggest problems, as voters continue to feel high living costs. Separate AP-NORC polling this month found only about one in six adults approving of his handling of the cost of living.

That creates a trap for Republican candidates in competitive races. They need Trump's most loyal voters to turn out, but embracing an unpopular president risks pushing away the independents they also need — a tension campaign strategists are now managing race by race.

Polls are a snapshot, not a result. With early voting already surging in several battleground states, the question for the next two weeks is whether these numbers harden into actual ballots.

items.title: The AI attack-ad nightmare is arriving: $137 million spent on 220 AI ads so far
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence is no longer a hypothetical worry in the midterms — it is in the ads voters are already seeing. Axios reported Monday that AI is producing reality-bending spots about defaced Bibles, upscale dinners and a board game with a 'Death to America' playing card, putting words in opponents' mouths and staging scenes that never happened.

The scale is now measurable. The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads through October 11, mostly from Republicans, according to the reporting. Some of the ads do not disclose that AI was used at all.

Election law has not kept up. There is no federal law that specifically regulates AI-generated political ads, and only a handful of states ban certain deepfake uses in campaigns, leaving a patchwork that varies by jurisdiction.

With two weeks to Election Day, the practical problem is speed: a fabricated clip can travel widely before any fact-check or correction catches it, which is why watchdogs say disclosure rules matter even when they cannot stop the ads outright.

items.title: Early voting is surging — Georgia up 40%, Ohio in-person voting more than doubled
items.summary:
Early voting is off to an unusually strong start across the battlegrounds. Georgia reported a 40% increase in first-day turnout compared with the 2022 midterms and more than double its 2018 opening day, while North Carolina and Maine are up about 38%, Iowa is up 61%, and Ohio's in-person early vote has more than doubled.

The split is in how people are voting. In-person voting is booming, but mail ballot returns are down — sharply in Georgia, down 58% in one measure, and down in Florida as well. Polling suggests falling confidence that the Postal Service will deliver ballots on time is part of that shift.

Voters interviewed in Georgia named the same cluster of motives pollsters keep finding nationally: inflation and prices, abortion access, immigration and a general desire for change. Democrats currently hold an early-participation edge in several key states, including North Carolina, Iowa and Pennsylvania.

Analysts caution that early leads describe who has voted, not who will win. Election Day turnout can still swamp the early numbers — but campaigns are treating the surge as a sign of an energized electorate on both sides.

items.title: Voters rank economy and cost of living far above every other midterm issue, AP-NORC finds
items.summary:
A new AP-NORC survey of voters finds the final stretch before the November 3 midterms dominated by one subject: 85% call the economy a major issue and 84% say the same about the cost of living. About half of voters are pessimistic about the future of both parties — and about democracy itself.

Overall, 36% of voters approve of President Trump's job performance while 64% disapprove. His strongest issue in the poll is crime, at 45% approval, while roughly three-quarters disapprove of his handling of the economy and four in five disapprove on the cost of living.

Asked who should control Congress, 47% favor Democrats in the House and 46% in the Senate, compared with 38% preferring Republicans in each chamber. Fifteen percent are unsure, with independents the most undecided group.

The poll of 1,119 adults was conducted October 8-12. Read alongside the weekend's other surveys, it tells a consistent story: prices are the issue, and they are the president's weakest ground.

items.title: Trump defends easing Russia sanctions as bipartisan anger in Congress continues
items.summary:
President Trump is continuing to defend his decision to waive a new package of Russia sanctions, a move that drew rare public criticism from lawmakers in both parties. Several Republicans called the waiver irresponsible and a concession that rewards Moscow while the war in Ukraine continues.

The White House argues that enforcing the sanctions now would interfere with talks aimed at a durable peace, and the president has pointed to energy prices and cooperation on Iran. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has described the diesel deal tied to the waiver as a peace incentive, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio has argued Russia would sell the fuel anyway.

Critics answer that earlier concessions were followed by more Russian attacks, not restraint, and Zelenskiy has warned that siding with Moscow would be a historic mistake. Monday's reporting from Moscow — where hard-liners are enjoying the Washington-Kyiv rift — will likely feature in that argument on Capitol Hill.

Congress is in recess until after the November elections, which limits how quickly lawmakers could try to override the waiver even if the votes existed.

items.title: The White House press secretary job is open again — and George Santos has volunteered
items.summary:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is transitioning out of the job after five days, a tenure reported as the shortest in the role's history, after the president told reporters he had advised her to reconsider her position.

Into that vacancy stepped an unlikely volunteer: former Rep. George Santos, who posted on X that he is not technically looking for a job but would jump to serve as press secretary in a heartbeat. A widely shared satirical post claiming he had already been appointed was false — no such announcement has been made.

Zacharia's brief run drew heavy scrutiny, including questions about her credentials and a first briefing that lasted under 15 minutes with questions from only three reporters.

There is no word yet on a successor. Whoever takes the podium will inherit a midterm-season communications job with very little runway.

items.title: Musk pledges one SpaceX share to every kid in America next year — a roughly $10.5 billion promise
items.summary:
Elon Musk posted early Monday that next year he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every kid in America, calling it the first of many such gifts. The post, made just before 4 a.m. Eastern, gave no mechanism, no eligibility definition and no date beyond next year.

The arithmetic is what makes the pledge enormous. There are roughly 72 million people under 18 in the United States, and SpaceX closed Friday around $146 a share, which puts the total value near $10.5 billion if under-18 is the cutoff. SpaceX went public in June in a record-setting IPO and trades under the ticker SPCX at a valuation near $2 trillion.

The idea did not come from nowhere. Musk posted it hours after Anthropic said it would commit a portion of its shares to a public benefit fund; Musk replied that he recommends giving shares directly to the public instead. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell earlier this year gifted about $325 million of stock into children's investment accounts, which offers one possible model.

Markets shrugged — SpaceX stock was essentially flat in premarket trading. The open questions are practical: whether the shares would use the new Trump Accounts for minors, how recipients would be identified, and how the tax side would work. SpaceX reports earnings Tuesday, which may be the first chance for a follow-up.

items.title: Stock futures bounce to start a huge earnings week: Meta, Tesla, Netflix and SpaceX all report
items.summary:
American stock futures rose Monday morning as buyers stepped back into technology shares after the market's worst week since late June. Futures tied to the Nasdaq were up about 1.3% and S&P 500 futures about 0.5% in the reporting, while Dow futures slipped slightly.

Two things outside tech helped the mood: oil eased — West Texas crude was down about 1% near $100 a barrel after surging Friday — and bitcoin recovered from a weekend low near $80,600 to about $82,500. The 10-year Treasury yield held around 5.10%, still high enough to keep pressure on growth stocks.

The calendar is now the story. Meta reports this week, Tesla follows on Wednesday, and SpaceX is scheduled to release results Tuesday, alongside Netflix, General Motors and GE Aerospace. Gold was little changed near $4,185 an ounce.

A one-morning bounce after a bad week is not a trend. This week's results will show whether companies are still spending freely on AI — and whether investors still applaud them for it.

items.title: Asia markets recover from an opening rout as China's growth data calms nerves
items.summary:
Asian markets mounted a broad intraday recovery on Monday, overcoming an opening selloff fueled by Wall Street's tech slide and worries about the cost of the AI buildout. Seoul's KOSPI had fallen about 3% early before closing up 1.76% at 5,768, and the smaller Kosdaq rose similarly.

Japan's Nikkei trimmed a 1,500-point opening drop to finish down just 0.62%, while Taiwan's index pared a 940-point fall to close down 0.61% as TSMC erased its losses to finish flat. Hong Kong markets were closed for the Chung Yeung Festival holiday, and South Korea's won touched its strongest level since October 2024.

Traders credited institutional dip-buying, state-backed funds and China's faster-than-expected 4.5% third-quarter growth for stabilizing sentiment. The region sits in the middle of the AI supply chain, so doubts about American data-center spending tend to hit it first — and relief travels just as fast.

The recovery does not settle the underlying argument about AI financing. It shows investors are willing to buy the dip while they wait for this week's American earnings to judge it.

items.title: Nvidia slips 1.4% to $214.13 — falling less than its chip rivals in the AI selloff
items.summary:
Nvidia shares fell 1.4% in the session covered by Monday's reporting, closing at $214.13 after trading between about $213 and $219. Volume reached roughly 121 million shares, about 12% above average, so the selling was heavier than usual even though the decline itself was modest by the week's standards.

In context, Nvidia held up better than most. The Nasdaq fell 2.15% in the same session, AMD dropped about 6%, Micron about 5.6% and Broadcom about 4.5%. Nvidia now sits about 12% below its 52-week high, with a market value around $5.16 trillion.

No company-specific cause was named for the decline. Weekend coverage focused on the financing behind the AI boom — including yields near 15% on bonds issued by cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia has invested — and on Amazon, Google and Microsoft expanding their own custom chips, a long-term competitive question for GPU demand.

Monday's premarket bounce in AI names suggests some investors see the selloff as overdone. Whether that holds will depend less on Nvidia itself than on the spending guidance in this week's earnings from its biggest customers.

items.title: Microsoft falls 1.9%, then a report says it walked away from a UK data-center deal over power delays
items.summary:
Microsoft shares fell 1.9% to $529.05 in the session covered Monday, opening above $541 before sellers took over. The decline was slightly milder than the Nasdaq's 2.15% drop, while Oracle fell about 4.6%, Meta about 3.7% and Amazon about 1.9% in the same session.

The move tracked a semiconductor-led selloff and broader worries about AI financing, rather than Microsoft-specific news during trading hours. A company headline arrived only after the close: Bloomberg, citing The Telegraph, reported Sunday that Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a planned data center in Loughton, Essex, where authorities had told the developer power might not arrive until the 2030s.

Microsoft did not comment, and a spokesman for the developer, Nscale, said its relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term. Even as an unconfirmed report, it illustrates the constraint now shaping the AI buildout in many places: not chips or capital, but electricity arriving on schedule.

That power question connects directly to debates much closer to home, including Cleveland's extended pause on new data centers while it writes permanent rules for grid and water use.

items.title: The Fed's new headache: the AI boom itself may be keeping inflation up
items.summary:
A Reuters analysis argues that the artificial intelligence boom has become a genuine problem for the Federal Reserve — the flood of spending on data centers, chips and power adds demand to the economy long before AI delivers productivity gains that would push prices down.

Central bankers gathering in Bangkok described the pattern openly: investment arrives first, benefits later. The Fed's chair called it a shock that hits the demand side before the supply side, and warned the transition could be bumpy.

That leaves the burden of tighter policy falling unevenly. Housing and ordinary businesses that borrow at today's rates feel the squeeze, while the biggest AI builders keep spending almost regardless of the rate — one reason markets now put meaningful odds on further tightening rather than cuts.

Some strategists see paths for inflation to cool anyway — cheaper oil if Middle East tensions ease, or a slower data-center buildout as local opposition grows — but none of them are painless or quick.

items.title: A new nor'easter forms off the Carolinas, threatening days of coastal flooding
items.summary:
A new low-pressure system forming off the Southeast coast is expected to bring several days of persistent onshore winds, coastal flooding and beach erosion from New Jersey through North Carolina, according to National Weather Service warnings summarized Monday.

Moderate coastal flooding is expected at Monday and Tuesday high tides, with one to four feet of inundation possible and gusts up to 60 mph. The worst erosion risk is in North Carolina's Outer Banks, and dangerous rip currents are forecast from Florida to New England through the week.

The system arrives while the saturated Southeast is still dealing with the aftermath of recent storms. Even without a landfalling hurricane, a slow nor'easter can do real damage by stacking high tides on top of each other day after day.

Residents in flood-prone coastal spots should expect road closures around high tide and check local forecasts before traveling. The pattern is expected to linger for days rather than pass in a single night.

items.title: Hurricane Trudy weakens off Mexico as Champi moves away from Guam and the Marianas
items.summary:
Hurricane Trudy began weakening rapidly Sunday after lashing parts of Mexico's Pacific coast with heavy rain and strong winds. The Category 1 storm had maximum sustained winds of about 80 mph and was moving northwest and away from the coast, with its center forecast to pass south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday.

Forecasters warned that further rain was still possible in areas where the ground is already saturated by successive storms, raising the risk of flooding and mudslides even as the winds ease.

In the western Pacific, Typhoon Champi has moved into the Philippine Sea and away from land for now, after passing close to Guam. President Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam, and FEMA said federal help is available to supplement local response — while warning relief supplies could take three to five days to reach the islands. Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed during the storm.

Champi has since re-strengthened over open water and is being watched for a later approach toward Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands later this week.

items.title: The federal deficit hit $1.99 trillion in fiscal 2026, the largest in five years
items.summary:
The Treasury reported that the federal budget deficit rose to $1.99 trillion for the fiscal year that ended September 30 — up from $1.78 trillion the year before and the largest shortfall since the pandemic-spending year of 2021.

Both sides of the ledger set records: the government took in $5.40 trillion and spent $7.40 trillion. The single fastest-growing burden is the interest bill itself, which reached a record $1.36 trillion and now trails only Social Security and the big health programs.

One surprise driver was tariffs — in reverse. After a Supreme Court ruling struck down a large share of the new tariffs, the government paid out about $145 billion in refunds, cutting net tariff income by 11%.

Total federal debt passed $40 trillion about two months ago. The deficit equaled roughly 6.2% of the economy, about double what analysts usually describe as a sustainable level — a backdrop both parties will argue over through the midterms.

items.title: America's $10 trillion AI buildout is starting to fray — and shoppers are wary of AI-set prices
items.summary:
Two sides of the AI economy drew attention Monday. On the building side, a Financial Times analysis found cracks appearing in America's debt-laden $10 trillion AI infrastructure boom, with at least 47 large data-center projects delayed, withdrawn or blocked in 2026 and more than 1,000 communities trying to introduce moratoria or other restrictions this year.

On the shopping side, consumers are pushing back on a quieter change: digital shelf tags replacing paper ones, and AI tools that help chains decide what to charge based on how customers are predicted to respond. Shoppers accept prices moving for flights and hotels; the anxiety starts when the same logic reaches groceries.

Large retailers and restaurant chains say critics misunderstand the tools, which they describe as ways to manage promotions and costs rather than charge individuals differently based on personal data. Lawmakers are not waiting to find out — proposals to limit personal-data use in pricing are already moving.

Together the stories show the buildout meeting its limits in public: towns questioning power and water use, and households questioning whether the price on the shelf is still the same price for everyone.
items.source: Financial Times / Associated Press via TFI Online

items.title: A service member dies after a rappelling fall before a college football game in San Antonio
items.summary:
A military service member died after falling while rappelling from the ceiling to midfield before the University of Texas at San Antonio's annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy on Saturday.

Nellis Air Force Base said the service member was assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2. He was taken to a local hospital, where he later died, with fans and a band already in the stadium.

Demonstrations like the pregame rappel are a familiar part of military appreciation games, which is part of why the accident has drawn wide attention — it happened during a ceremonial moment, in front of a crowd, rather than in training out of public view.

An investigation is under way into what led to the fall. The service has not released further detail about the failure point.
items.source: Associated Press via Rapid City Post

items.title: Guardians name Shawn Armstrong as Game 6 opener — his third appearance in three days
items.summary:
Cleveland made its Game 6 pitching plan official Monday morning: veteran reliever Shawn Armstrong will start and open tonight's elimination game against Tampa Bay at Tropicana Field, with first pitch at 8:08 p.m. ET on TBS and truTV.

Armstrong has earned the trust. He opened Game 4 on Saturday with a scoreless first inning, came back Sunday to throw 1 1/3 more scoreless innings in Game 5, and has not allowed a run in 7 2/3 innings this postseason. The catch is workload — tonight will be his third appearance in three days, so he is likely to face the top of the Rays' lineup only once before the bullpen takes over.

Manager Stephen Vogt had already ruled out ace Gavin Williams on short rest, keeping him lined up for a potential Game 7 on Tuesday. Tampa Bay counters with Freddy Peralta, who threw six scoreless innings against Cleveland in Game 2 and has not allowed more than one earned run in any of his last eight starts.

The math is simple and unforgiving: win tonight and tomorrow, or the season ends in Florida. The World Series starts Friday in Milwaukee against the Brewers.

items.title: 'Let's go. We don't have another choice' — Guardians embrace another 3-2 comeback try
items.summary:
The Guardians have been here before, and they are leaning on that history. Down three games to two after Sunday's 3-1 loss, with no travel day because of an earlier rainout, Cleveland needs two road wins in two nights to reach the World Series.

Manager Stephen Vogt's message was short: this is when this team thrives. Steven Kwan, who had two of Cleveland's five hits in Game 5 plus his first career postseason outfield assist, said the experience of the last comeback helps — the Guardians dropped the first two Division Series games at home to Chicago, then won two on the road and closed it out at home.

Cleveland's September is part of the belief, too. The Guardians were 60-65 and 5 1/2 games behind the White Sox in mid-August before winning the division by one game, their second straight late-season rally to a Central title.

None of that changes tonight's matchup problem — Peralta on the mound for Tampa Bay and a Cleveland offense that scored once on Sunday — but it explains why nobody in the clubhouse is treating Game 6 as a funeral.

items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs stock jumps more than 10% after its strongest quarter in three years
items.summary:
Cleveland-based steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs gave investors a morning jolt Monday: shares rose more than 10% after the company reported third-quarter results ahead of expectations and raised its outlook. Adjusted earnings were $0.28 a share against estimates around $0.24, on revenue of about $5.61 billion, up roughly 18.5% from a year earlier.

Chief executive Lourenco Goncalves called it the company's strongest quarter in three years, with adjusted EBITDA of $612 million beating the $575 million guidance given three months ago. Cliffs shipped about 4.2 million net tons of steel at an average selling price of $1,177 per ton, and held $3.2 billion in liquidity at the end of September.

Management guided fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA to about $715 million and said 2027 could exceed $4 billion on new contract pricing, while reaffirming a target of cutting net debt relative to earnings below 2.5 times by mid-2027.

For northern Ohio, Cliffs is a bellwether: its product mix — hot-rolled steel first, then coated products, much of it for autos — ties its results directly to the manufacturing economy across the region.

items.title: Ohio governor's race: Acton leads Ramaswamy in most polls — and says she will never debate him
items.summary:
Ohio's governor's race tightened into its final two weeks with Democrat Amy Acton ahead in most recent polling. Averages in mid-October put Acton near 48.7% to Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's roughly 43.7%, though one recent survey gave Ramaswamy a narrow lead and the major race raters — Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball — all call it a toss-up.

The race also produced a striking non-debate. Acton told The Vindicator she will never stand on a stage with Ramaswamy, accusing him of egregious and chronic lying. Ramaswamy said he was shocked to learn she would not debate.

Money tells its own story. Ramaswamy has lent his campaign more than $36 million, including over $5 million in August and September, while Acton raised slightly more than $6 million in September against just over $3 million raised by Ramaswamy in the same period. The next campaign finance reports are due October 23.

One number in the polling should worry Republicans: among voters who backed Trump in 2024, about 24% said they regretted their vote. Early voting in Ohio is already under way ahead of the November 3 election.

items.title: Solon Council votes tonight on $13.2 million in park and trail notes
items.summary:
Tonight's Solon City Council meeting is the decision point for two borrowing ordinances that have been working through readings this month: $7.2 million in notes for Solon Community Park and $6 million for the Norfolk Southern Headwaters Connector Trail.

Both measures got their second reading on October 5, and tonight is the meeting where they become actionable — and the last scheduled chance for residents to comment before a vote. Council earlier slowed the combined package down, holding it in September to take more time.

The park money follows the Community Park's reopening and fall festival earlier this month, while the trail notes would advance a connector project residents have watched for several seasons.

Also on residents' minds tonight: three charter amendments headed to the November ballot. If you care about either the borrowing or the amendments, tonight at City Hall is the night to say so.

items.title: Cleveland wants to extend its pause on new data centers into early 2027
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council is moving to extend the city's temporary pause on new standalone data centers until January 29, 2027. The current three-month moratorium was set to expire October 20.

The pause grew out of a council working group and three town halls, where residents raised questions about zoning, the power grid and water use. Those are not abstract concerns in Ohio: the state already has dozens of operating data centers and far more planned, most of the growth concentrated around Columbus.

Cleveland is not alone — one tracking count put the number of local data-center moratoriums statewide at 125 as of September. Communities are using the breathing room to write permanent rules instead of approving projects one at a time.

The extension heads to the Finance Committee next, then to the full council. Whatever rules come out of it will shape where the AI building boom is — and is not — welcome inside city limits.
